2.	The overall increase of $1.3 million for the 15 continuing special political missions is attributable primarily to: (a) increased requirements for civilian personnel resulting from the application of lower vacancy rates and the application of the latest salary rates; and (b) increased requirements for expert fees, reflecting changes in the budgeted average monthly fees based on the current composition of expert teams. The increase was offset in part by: (a) lower estimated common staff costs for national staff, based on actual past expenditures; and (b) reduced requirements for communications and information technology, reflecting the non-recurrent provision for the acquisition of equipment included in the 2026 approved budget, as well as lower requirements for subscriptions to specialized databases and news resources to support and supplement investigations and research.
Vacancy rates

3.	The proposed vacancy rates applied in the budget take into account the experience to date. The assumptions considered for the proposed vacancy factors include: (a) the 12-month average vacancy rate from January to December 2025; and (b) the actual vacancy rate as at 31 March 2026. The lower of the two was used as the budgeted vacancy rate. This is in line with the policy guidance to improve the accuracy and consistency of the vacancy factors applied in the proposed budgets for 2027 and to ensure that the proposed vacancy rates are based, as much as possible, on actual rates. Annex II outlines the proposed vacancy rates.
Efficiency gains

4.	The proposed budget reflects efficiencies and cost-reductions measures resulting in reduced requirements for operational costs owing to: (a) lower official and expert travel requirements through the use of virtual meetings and the consolidation of travel itineraries, where feasible, and efficiencies achieved through the use of regional meeting formats with intelligence counterparts by the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team (Monitoring Team). Specifically, by expanding participation and representation at these regional meetings, the Monitoring Team was able to broaden its outreach and use expert travel resources more efficiently through a decreased number of country-specific visits; (b) reduced requirements under facilities and infrastructure for the rental of office equipment due to the consolidation of previously dispersed work locations for New York-based staff across Cluster II special political missions administered by the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs; (c) reduced provisions for security services taking into account partial close protection support provided by BINUH during visits to Haiti; and (d) lower requirements under communications and information technology, resulting from the discontinuation of fixed telephone services following increased reliance on internet-based communication technologies.

5.	For the sake of brevity, the present document will include a section on extrabudgetary resources only for those missions that have projected extrabudgetary resources in 2026 or 2027.
Cooperation

6.	To improve the effectiveness of sanctions imposed by the Security Council, the missions supporting sanctions committees will, as requested, engage with the Informal Working Group of the Security Council on General United Nations Security Council Sanctions Issues established by resolution 2744 (2024).
Gender perspective

7.	Special political missions are guided by the relevant Security Council resolutions on the women and peace and security agenda, which mandate the incorporation of a gender perspective into the political work of the United Nations, including in special political missions. The missions are also guided by General Assembly resolution 75/100 on the comprehensive review of special political missions, in which the Assembly reaffirmed the important role of women in the prevention and resolution of conflicts and in peacebuilding and recognized the importance of the equal and effective participation and the full involvement of women at all levels, at all stages and in all aspects of the peaceful settlement of disputes, conflict prevention and conflict resolution.

8.	The sanctions monitoring teams, groups and panels, along with the mission supporting the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1718 (2006), integrate a gender perspective into their operational activities, deliverables and results, as guided by the relevant Security Council resolutions. Gender balance is an important consideration in the recruitment of experts, the Focal Point for Delisting and the Ombudsperson, as well as related staff. The terms of reference for experts in sanctions monitoring teams, groups and panels indicate that experts are to incorporate gender perspectives into their substantive areas of responsibility. In addition, the Focal Point for Delisting will examine delisting petitions in relation to relevant designation criteria, referring to sexual and gender-based violence.

9.	These missions are also guided by the gender strategy of the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs and benefit from available gender training for staff and sanctions-specific gender training for experts. To further broaden the geographical and gender diversity of sanctions monitoring teams, groups and panels, in October 2025, the Department participated in the ImpactPool virtual career fair for women in senior roles. A total of 914 women registered for the career fair, 410 of whom (from countries across all regional groups) visited the Department’s virtual booth containing presentations, fact sheets, videos and information on job openings for sanctions experts. In addition, in May 2025, the Department briefed representatives of the Group of Asia-Pacific States and, in February 2026, the Group of African States, on the recruitment process of members of sanctions monitoring teams, groups and panels.
Disability inclusion

10.	In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, special political missions review the Strategy with a view to further advancing disability inclusion through inclusive messaging, awareness-raising and promoting the Strategy through their work, including in political and peace processes. The missions also support mitigating measures to overcome accessibility challenges, in addition to the efforts by relevant United Nations entities to ensure the accessibility of facilities, platforms, security and other infrastructure to facilitate easy access and use by persons with disabilities.
Evaluation activities

11.	The Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs will support the biennial assessment conducted by the Office of Internal Oversight Services on strengthening the role of evaluation and the application of evaluation findings on programme design, delivery and policy directives. Mission-specific evaluation activities are described, as applicable, under the respective missions in the present report.
1.	Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

12.	The Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo is responsible for monitoring the implementation of the arms embargo, asset freeze, travel ban and transport and customs measures, as well as for providing information relevant to the potential designation of individuals and entities. The mandate derives from the priorities established in relevant Security Council resolutions, including resolution 1533 (2004), and renewed in its subsequent resolutions, including, most recently, resolution 2783 (2025). The sanctions regime is aimed at preventing individuals and entities from undermining the peace, stability or security of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Programme of work
Objective

13.	The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to ensure the full implementation of the sanctions regime concerning the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which includes an arms embargo on all non-governmental entities and individuals operating in the territory of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, an asset freeze and a travel ban.
Strategy and external factors for 2027

14.	To contribute to the objective, the Group of Experts will provide updated information to the Security Council and the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1533 (2004) concerning the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
15.	The above-mentioned work is expected to result in an enhanced capacity of the Security Council and the Committee to take follow-up action on alleged violations of the sanctions regime.

16.	With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission cooperates with, among others, Member States and the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region to request information relevant to its investigations into the implementation and/or violations of the sanctions regime concerning the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

17.	With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Group of Experts cooperates with, among others, the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Focal Point for Delisting to support the review of petitioners’ requests to be removed from the Committee’s sanctions list, the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict, the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Sexual Violence in Conflict and other sanctions monitoring teams, groups and panels, as appropriate. In the context of safety, security and logistics, the Group of Experts cooperates with the Mission, the Department of Safety and Security and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).
18.	With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	Member States comply with the resolutions of the Security Council and cooperate with the Group of Experts;
(b)	The security situation allows the Group of Experts to conduct missions, as needed.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

19.	The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects changes arising from the UN80 Initiative. In particular, the tables of deliverables reflect updated planned deliverables for 2026, in line with the approved programme budget for 2026.
Programme performance in 2025
Enhanced understanding by the Security Council and the Committee of the illegal exploitation of natural resources and the activities of armed groups in the Democratic Republic of the Congo

20.	The Group of Experts reported on the activities of armed groups and criminal networks in destabilizing the Democratic Republic of the Congo through the illegal exploitation of or trade in natural resources and in that regard recommended that States cooperate fully with the ad hoc Commission of Inquiry established by the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region to investigate allegations of smuggling of tin, tantalum and tungsten minerals and gold.

21.	This work contributed to the Security Council and the Committee receiving updated information on the involvement of armed groups and criminal networks in the illicit exploitation of and trade in natural resources, including criminal networks’ role in financing armed groups, exacerbating insecurity and negatively affecting civilian populations.

Enhanced understanding by the Security Council and the Committee of the illegal activities of armed groups in the Democratic Republic of the Congo – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

23.	In 2025, the work of the Group of Experts contributed to the full implementation of the sanctions regime, which met the planned target. In its midterm report (S/2025/858), the Group of Experts reported that despite ongoing negotiations following the signing of peace agreements, their implementation had stalled as armed groups continued mobilizing and conducting offensive operations. Alliance Fleuve Congo/Mouvement du 23 mars (AFC/M23) expanded its territorial control across North and South Kivu in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and conducted operations against the Forces démocratiques de libération du Rwanda (FDLR) with support from the Rwandan Defence Forces. AFC/M23 also consolidated access to major mining sites.

Overall orientation
Mandates and background

30.	The Panel of Experts on the Sudan is responsible for monitoring the implementation of the arms embargo, asset freeze and travel ban, as well as for providing information relevant to the potential designation of individuals and entities. The mandate is defined in Security Council resolution 1591 (2005) and renewed in its subsequent resolutions, including, most recently, 2791 (2025). The sanctions regime is one of the tools used by the Council to address the conflict in Darfur and is aimed at preventing threats to the stability in Darfur and the region, towards a peaceful settlement of the conflict in Darfur. In its resolution 2791 (2025), the Council extended the mandate of the mission until 12 October 2026.
Programme of work
Objective

31.	The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to ensure the full implementation of the sanctions regime concerning the Sudan, which includes an arms embargo, an asset freeze and a travel ban, as well as to report on the possible threats to the peace and stability of Darfur, including the current conflict.

34.	With regard to cooperation with other entities, the Panel of Experts cooperates with, among others, Member States and the African Union.

35.	With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Panel of Experts cooperates with, among others, the Focal Point for Delisting to support the review of petitioners’ requests to be removed from the Committee’s sanctions list, the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, the United Nations Children’s Fund, the Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Sudan, and other sanctions monitoring teams, groups and panels, as appropriate. 3.	Support to the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1718 (2006)
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

47.	The Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1718 (2006) oversees the implementation of the sanctions regime concerning the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. The sanctions regime is the most comprehensive and complex of all United Nations sanctions regimes in effect and is intended to ensure that the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea abandons all nuclear weapons and its existing nuclear programme, as well as any other existing weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programmes, in a complete, verifiable and irreversible manner. The regime includes 26 sanctions measures. In addition to an arms embargo and an embargo relating to nuclear, ballistic missile and other weapons of mass destruction programmes, a travel ban and/or asset freeze on designated individuals and entities, it includes a range of maritime provisions for designating vessels for involvement in prohibited activities and restrictions on various commodity transfers, such as refined petroleum products, minerals, metals, heavy machinery, transportation vehicles, luxury goods, seafood, textiles and more. It also includes restrictions on transportation and on financial services, as well as on overseas workers. Furthermore, the Security Council adopted a wide range of humanitarian and other exemptions to ensure that the imposed measures do not have adverse humanitarian consequences for the civilian population.

48.	The support of the Secretariat is required across all areas of the Committee’s mandate. Member States and other actors liaise directly with the Committee and the Secretariat for guidance on, or assistance with, the implementation of sanctions measures, including exemptions and notifications, which were previously handled by the Panel of Experts. The Committee and the Secretariat receive a high volume of information on alleged violations of the sanctions measures, which were also previously handled by the Panel. In addition, the Chair and the Committee undertake increased outreach activities to promote better understanding and implementation of the relevant resolutions, including the various exemptions processes. The Secretariat also provides extensive guidance in responding to requests from Member States, the United Nations and humanitarian actors.

49.	Furthermore, with the gradual return of the international community to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, there has been an increase in humanitarian exemption requests received by the Committee.
Programme of work
Objective

50.	The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to ensure the full implementation of the sanctions regime concerning the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, which includes an arms embargo, an embargo relating to nuclear, ballistic missile and other weapons of mass destruction programmes, an asset freeze, a travel ban, maritime and financial measures, a ban on petroleum products and crude oil, a coal ban and sanctions measures in other sectoral areas.
Strategy and external factors for 2027

51.	To contribute to the objective, the mission will continue to support the work of the Security Council and the Committee in relation to the implementation of the sanctions regime with regard to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

52.	The above-mentioned work is expected to result in an enhanced capacity of the Security Council and the Committee conducive to overseeing and promoting the full implementation of the Council sanctions measures.

53.	With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission will continue to cooperate with the Resident Coordinator’s Office and the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs and other United Nations agencies carrying out humanitarian assistance and relief activities in the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, including the Food and Agriculture Organization, UNDP, the United Nations Population Fund, the United Nations Children’s Fund, WFP and the World Health Organization, as well as other non-United Nations agencies carrying out related activities. The mission will continue to facilitate the work of the United Nations agencies through regular and ad hoc briefings to the United Nations country team in the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, and assist those agencies with the Committee’s humanitarian exemption application process. The mission will also continue to guide relevant entities through the sanctions measures and exemption procedures to ensure sanctions compliance. In the context of safety and security, information technology security and logistics, the mission cooperates with the Department of Safety and Security and the Office of Information and Communications Technology.
54.	With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	Member States will comply with the resolutions of the Security Council and continue to cooperate with the sanctions committee;
(b)	The Chair and the Committee are adequately supported to perform their functions as mandated by the Security Council.

57.	The above-mentioned work contributed to the Security Council’s and the Committee’s ability to oversee the implementation of sanctions as the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea persisted in carrying out prohibited activities, including ballistic missile launches.

Overall orientation
Mandates and background

66.	The Panel of Experts on Libya is responsible for monitoring the implementation of the arms embargo, asset freeze, travel ban and measures in relation to attempts to illicitly export petroleum, and for providing information relevant to the potential designation of individuals and entities. The mandate derives from the priorities established in relevant Security Council resolutions, including resolutions 1973 (2011), 2009 (2011) and 2017 (2011), and renewed in its subsequent resolutions, including, most recently, 2819 (2026). The sanctions regime is aimed at preventing and containing threats to the peace, security and stability of Libya, including obstructing or undermining the successful completion of the political transition. In its resolutions 2780 (2025) and 2804 (2025), the Council requested the Secretary-General to report on the implementation of the arms embargo on the high seas off the coast of Libya. The Secretary-General submitted his first report on 27 October 2025 (S/2025/675), while the second report was submitted on 22 April 2026 (S/2026/354).

67.	In its resolution 2769 (2025), the Security Council authorized the frozen cash reserves of the Libyan Investment Authority to be invested in low-risk time deposits and in fixed financial instruments, subject to a notification and approval procedure by the Sanctions Committee concerning Libya, and requested the Panel of Experts to assess the effect and performance of those investments in their annual final reports.
Programme of work
Objective

(a)	Member States comply with the resolutions of the Security Council and cooperate with the Panel of Experts;

7.	Panel of Experts on South Sudan
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

118.	The Panel of Experts on South Sudan is responsible for monitoring the implementation of the arms embargo, asset freeze and travel ban, as well as for providing information relevant to the potential designation of individuals and entities. The mandate derives from the priorities established in relevant Security Council resolutions, including resolution 2206 (2015), and renewed in its subsequent resolutions, including, most recently, 2781 (2025). The sanctions regime is aimed at, but not limited to, targeting spoilers of the Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in the Republic of South Sudan, which was signed on 12 September 2018. On 16 April 2026, following a request by the Council in its resolution 2731 (2024), the Secretary-General provided the Council with an assessment of the progress achieved on the key benchmarks established in resolution 2577 (2021) (S/2026/330).
Programme of work
Objective

119.	The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to ensure the full implementation of the sanctions regime concerning South Sudan, which includes a territorial arms embargo, an asset freeze and a travel ban.
Strategy and external factors for 2027

120.	To contribute to the objective, the Panel of Experts will provide updated information, including on the potential impacts of elections currently scheduled for December 2026, on the overall situation in South Sudan, to the Security Council and the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 2206 (2015) concerning South Sudan.

121.	The above-mentioned work is expected to result in an enhanced capacity of the Security Council and the Committee to take follow-up action on alleged violations of the sanctions regime, including actions or policies that threaten the peace, security or stability of South Sudan.

122.	With regard to cooperation with other entities, in the context of information-sharing, the Panel of Experts cooperates with, among others, Member States, the African Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development.

123.	With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Panel of Experts cooperates with the United Nations Mission in South Sudan, the Focal Point for Delisting to support the review of petitioners’ requests to be removed from the Committee’s sanctions list, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict, the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Sexual Violence in Conflict and other sanctions monitoring teams, groups and panels, as appropriate. In the context of safety and security, information technology security and logistics, the Panel cooperates with the Mission, the Department of Safety and Security and UNDP.
124.	With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	Member States comply with the resolutions of the Security Council and cooperate with the Panel of Experts;
(b)	The security situation allows the Panel of Experts to conduct missions, as needed.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

125. 	The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects changes arising from the UN80 Initiative. In particular, the tables of deliverables reflect updated planned deliverables for 2026, in line with the approved programme budget for 2026.
Programme performance in 2025
Committee members receive an update on the implementation of the Revitalized Agreement and on the progress made in the implementation of the key benchmarks of the arms embargo

126.	The Panel of Experts provided the Security Council and the Committee with information on the implementation of the Revitalized Agreement, focusing on the political and security crisis since March 2025, including the detention and trial of prominent opposition leaders, among them First Vice President Riek Machar, and the resulting escalation of armed clashes between government and opposition security forces. This information enabled Committee members to assess the impact of the crisis on transitional security arrangements, a key element for completing South Sudan’s transitional period through February 2027.

A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

135.	The Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team, which supports the work of both the Security Council Committee pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) concerning Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant (Da’esh), Al-Qaida and associated individuals, groups, undertakings and entities (ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions Committee), and the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1988 (2011), is responsible for assisting in and reporting on the implementation of asset freezes, travel bans and targeted arms embargoes on designated individuals and entities. The mandate is derived from the priorities established in the relevant Council resolutions, including resolution 1267 (1999), which was renewed in its subsequent resolutions, including, most recently, 2734 (2024), 2761 (2024), 2763 (2024) and 2816 (2025). The sanctions regimes are aimed at strengthening the Council’s response to threats to international peace and security caused by terrorist acts and at contributing to the peace, stability and security of Afghanistan.

Objective

136.	The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to ensure the full implementation of sanctions regimes concerning Da’esh, Al-Qaida and the Taliban, which include targeted arms embargoes, asset freezes and travel bans.

The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to provide an independent review of delisting requests of individuals, entities and undertakings on the ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida sanctions list. In doing so, it ensures that listed individuals, entities and undertakings have access to fair and clear procedures for the administration of requests for removal (delisting) from the sanctions list.

154.	To contribute to the objective, the Office will fairly and expeditiously consider and process all requests for delisting and travel to interview each petitioner in person, whenever possible, in the petitioner’s country of residence.

155.	The above-mentioned work is expected to result in informed decision-making by the Committee on the Ombudsperson’s analysis and recommendation on the delisting request contained in a comprehensive report on each case.

156.	With regard to cooperation with other entities, including in the context of information-sharing, the Office cooperates with, among others, Member States, the European Union, academic institutions, think tanks and international law associations.

157.	With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office cooperates with, among others, UNDP, OHCHR, the Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate, the Office of Counter-Terrorism, the Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms while countering terrorism, and the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team pursuant to resolutions 1526 (2004) and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da’esh), Al-Qaida and the Taliban and associated individuals and entities. In the context of safety and security, information technology security and logistics, the Office cooperates with the Department of Safety and Security, the Office of Information and Communications Technology and UNDP.
158.	With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	Member States comply with the resolutions of the Security Council and cooperate with the Office;
(b)	The security situation allows the Office to conduct missions, as needed.

10.	Panel of Experts pursuant to resolution 2713 (2023)
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

170.	The Panel of Experts pursuant to resolution 2713 (2023) is responsible for monitoring the implementation of the asset freeze, the travel ban, the targeted arms embargo and the territorial arms embargo focused on Al-Shabaab, the charcoal ban and the improvised explosive device components restrictions, as well as for providing information relevant to the designation of individuals and entities. Its mandate is referenced in Security Council resolution 2444 (2018), and renewed in its subsequent resolutions, including, most recently, 2806 (2025). The sanctions regime is aimed at supporting the efforts of the Somali authorities to deliver stability and security in Somalia, to prevent any flows of weapons and ammunition to Al-Shabaab and other actors undermining peace and security in Somalia and the region, and to disrupt Al-Shabaab’s activities and finances.

171.	On 24 October 2025, following the request by the Security Council in resolution 2776 (2025), the Secretary-General provided a technical assessment of the arms embargo targeting Al-Shabaab (S/2025/673) with specific recommendations. In resolution 2806 (2025), the Council requested the Secretary-General to submit a further technical assessment regarding the arms embargo targeting Al-Shabaab by 31 October 2026.
Programme of work
Objective

172.	The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to ensure the full implementation of the sanctions regime concerning Al-Shabaab, which includes an asset freeze, a travel ban, targeted and territorial arms embargoes, a charcoal ban and improvised explosive device components restrictions.
Strategy and external factors for 2027

173.	To contribute to the objective, the Panel of Experts will provide updated information to the Security Council and the Security Council Committee pursuant to resolution 2713 (2023) concerning Al-Shabaab.
174.	The above-mentioned work is expected to result in an enhanced capacity of the Security Council and the Committee to take follow-up action on alleged violations of the sanctions regime.

175.	With regard to cooperation with other entities, in the context of information-sharing, the Panel of Experts cooperates with, among others, Member States, INTERPOL, the African Union and the European Union. It also cooperates with the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia.

176.	With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Panel of Experts cooperates with, among others, the United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia, the United Nations Support Office in Somalia, the United Nations Office at Nairobi, UNODC, other sanctions monitoring teams, groups and panels, as appropriate, and the Focal Point for Delisting to support the review of petitioners’ requests to be removed from the Committee’s sanctions list. In the context of safety, security and logistics, the Panel cooperates with the Department of Safety and Security and security teams of the United Nations Office at Nairobi, the United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia, the United Nations Support Office in Somalia and UNDP.
177.	With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	Member States comply with the resolutions of the Security Council and cooperate with the Panel of Experts;
(b)	The security situation allows the Panel of Experts to conduct missions, as needed.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

178.	The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects changes arising from the UN80 Initiative. In particular, the tables of deliverables reflect updated planned deliverables for 2026, in line with the approved programme budget for 2026.
Programme performance in 2025
Enhanced capacity of the Security Council, the Committee and Member States to counter Al-Shabaab financing

179.	In 2025, in its final report (S/2025/777), the Panel of Experts assessed that the threat of Al-Shabaab remains the most immediate threat to the peace, security and stability of Somalia and the region. In Somalia, the threat goes beyond the impact of conventional military action and asymmetric warfare to include sophisticated extortion, forced recruitment practices and an effective propaganda machine. The Panel further documented that Abdullahi Wadad had been appointed as a new finance emir of Al-Shabaab, and the group continued to extort in areas outside its influence, including in Mogadishu.

12.	Office of the Focal Point for Delisting
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

206.	The mandate of the Office of the Focal Point for Delisting derives from Security Council resolution 1730 (2006), in which the Council adopted a delisting procedure and requested the Secretary-General to establish a Focal Point. The mandate was extended in its subsequent resolutions 2083 (2012), 2161 (2014) and 2255 (2015) and, most recently, strengthened in resolution 2744 (2024). The Focal Point is mandated to review delisting requests from individuals, groups, undertakings or entities designated on the lists of the sanctions committees established by the Council, excluding the sanctions list of the ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions Committee which falls under the purview of the Office of the Ombudsperson established pursuant to Security Council resolution 1904 (2009). The Focal Point is also mandated to deal with requests for travel ban and asset freeze exemptions, and communications related to cases of false or mistaken identity and post-delisting challenges, from specific listed individuals or entities.
Programme of work
Objective

207.	The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to provide an independent review of delisting requests submitted by, or on behalf of, an individual, group, undertaking or entity designated on the lists of the sanctions committees established by the Security Council (the petitioner), excluding the ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions Committee, in accordance with annex I to resolution 2744 (2024).
Strategy and external factors for 2027

208.	To contribute to the objective, the Focal Point will carry out the tasks set out in the delisting procedures detailed in annex I to resolution 2744 (2024), which provides an outline of the process for information-gathering, dialogue and committee discussion and decision upon receipt of a delisting request, and in other relevant resolutions.

209.	The above-mentioned work is expected to result in strengthened due process in Security Council sanctions regimes, through fair and clear delisting procedures, and the timely processing of requests for delisting, travel ban and asset freeze exemptions, as well as communications related to cases of false or mistaken identity and post-delisting challenges.

210.	With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional and local levels, including in the context of information-sharing, the Focal Point will cooperate with Member States, such as members of the Security Council, and the designating State(s) and State(s) of residence and nationality or incorporation of the petitioners.

211.	With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Focal Point will cooperate with any relevant sanctions committee’s groups or panels of experts or monitoring teams, as well as any relevant United Nations envoys engaged in negotiations and peace processes relevant to the sanctions. In the context of safety and security, information technology security and logistics, the Focal Point will also cooperate with the Department of Safety and Security, the Office of Information and Communications Technology and UNDP.

212.	To improve the effectiveness of sanctions imposed by the Security Council, the Focal Point will, as requested, engage with the Informal Working Group of the Security Council on General United Nations Security Council Sanctions Issues established pursuant to resolution 2744 (2024).
213.	With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	Member States comply with the resolutions of the Security Council and cooperate with the mission;
(b)	The security situation allows the mission to conduct missions, as needed;
(c)	Petitioners and other relevant actors are aware of the new delisting procedure outlined in resolution 2744 (2024).

A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025

Mandates and background

225.	The Panel of Experts on the Islamic Republic of Iran is responsible for monitoring the implementation of the embargo related to proliferation-sensitive nuclear activities and development of nuclear weapon delivery systems; arms embargo; restrictions on enrichment, reprocessing or heavy-water-related activities; travel ban; asset freeze; ban on bunkering services, financial services, and training or assistance; as well as providing information relevant to the designation of individuals and entities. The mandate of the Panel derives from the priorities established in Security Council resolutions 1696 (2006), 1737 (2006), 1747 (2007), 1803 (2008), 1835 (2008) and 1929 (2010), as reinstated on 27 September 2025 until 26 September 2026, pursuant to paragraphs 11 and 12 of resolution 2231 (2015). The sanctions regime aims to ensure that the Islamic Republic of Iran halts all its uranium enrichment and other activities related to the development of nuclear weapons and fully complies with its obligations under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and relevant safeguards agreements with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

14.	Support to the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1540 (2004) on the non-proliferation of all weapons of mass destruction
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

243.	The mission in support of the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1540 (2004) is responsible for the provision of substantive, administrative, technical, and logistical support to assist the Committee in achieving the aims of the resolution as well as subsequent resolutions. The mandate derives from Council resolution 1540 (2004) and from its subsequent resolutions, including, most recently, 2663 (2022), by which the Security Council extended the 1540 Committee’s mandate until 30 November 2032. The mission assists requesting Member States in their national implementation efforts through activities such as country-specific visits and dialogues, workshops and peer reviews, with the objective of building capacity, developing voluntary 1540 national action plans, facilitating assistance and identifying and disseminating effective practices for the implementation of resolution 1540 (2004). The mission specifically supports the work of the Committee through the organization of regional and subregional workshops, including national 1540 points of contact training courses, on the implementation of the resolution and through country-specific missions and activities, cooperation between international and regional bodies, and the facilitation of outreach and effective partnerships with civil society and the private sector.

244.	In its resolution 2663 (2022), the Security Council further decided that the 1540 Committee would conduct comprehensive reviews on the status of implementation of resolution 1540 (2004), including through the holding of open consultations of the Committee in New York, with the first review (after the adoption of resolution 2663) to be held before December 2027, and would submit to the Council a report upon the conclusion of each of the review. Preparatory work for the review is underway.
Programme of work
Objective

245.	The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to prevent non-State actors from developing, acquiring, manufacturing, possessing, transporting, transferring or using nuclear, chemical or biological weapons and their means of delivery.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
246.	To contribute to the objective, the mission will:

(a)	Facilitate assistance to Member States, upon their request, which includes support for national reviews of the status of implementation of resolution 1540 (2004), the development and updating of national implementation action plans, and relevant capacity-building and awareness-raising activities to enhance the implementation of resolution 1540 (2004);

(b)	Promote regional cooperation in the implementation of resolution 1540 (2004) by conducting regional, subregional and cross-regional activities, with priority given to training for points of contact;

(c)	Prepare for and conduct the 2027 comprehensive review, including activities to take stock of progress since the 2022 review, identify gaps and evaluate needs, and support implementation of the outcome of the 2027 review, including through the effective mobilization of necessary resources.
247.	The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
(a)	Enhanced national capacity to implement resolution 1540 (2004);
(b)	An increased number of reports, updates of reports, and national implementation action plans submitted to the 1540 Committee;
(c)	Concrete progress made on the implementation of adopted national action plans;

(d)	Increased awareness of resolution 1540 (2004) and the importance of its implementation to address the risks posed by non-State actors acquiring access to weapons of mass destruction and their means of delivery;
(e)	Increased cooperation among regional partners, including through peer-review, in implementing resolution 1540 (2004);
(f)	Successful conduct of the 2027 comprehensive review of the status of implementation of resolution 1540 (2004).

248.	With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission cooperates with Governments, international, regional and subregional organizations, civil society organizations and other relevant partners to raise awareness of the obligations under resolution 1540 (2004). It also facilitates assistance to Member States, upon request, to build capacity, including through support in drafting legislation, in order to enhance implementation of the resolution.

249.	With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission works closely with other relevant United Nations entities whose mandates address the risks of the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction to non-State actors. The inter‑entity process organized by the mission aims to enhance programme implementation and coordination by facilitating collaboration and the efficient use of resources.

250.	The mission also cooperates with the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1373 (2001) concerning counter-terrorism and its Executive Directorate, as well as the Security Council Committee pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) concerning Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant (Da’esh), Al-Qaida and associated individuals, groups, undertakings and entities, and the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team supporting that Committee, including through support for regular joint briefings to the Security Council by the three Committees.
251.	With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	The proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and their means of delivery to non-State actors remains a threat to international peace and security;
(b)	Members of the 1540 Committee continue to be able to reach agreement on the implementation of planned activities;
(c)	Member States continue to demonstrate political commitment to implementing resolution 1540, while expressing an ongoing need for assistance;
(d)	Assistance providers and the donor community continue to offer support to implement resolution 1540 (2004);
252.	The mission integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate, and is guided by the gender policy of the Office for Disarmament Affairs.

253.	The mission, in support of the Committee, promotes diversity and inclusion and ensures inclusive programming throughout its work, including the inclusion of disability perspectives and other reinforcing factors, such as gender and age. The mission promotes an inclusive work environment that enables all stakeholders to participate fully and effectively in disarmament forums and processes.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

254.	The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the mission to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.
Programme performance in 2025
Strengthened capacity of Member States requesting assistance to implement resolution 1540 through needs-based assistance activities and enhanced international cooperation

15.	Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

266.	The Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate is mandated to support the Counter-Terrorism Committee in its work to monitor, promote and facilitate the implementation by Member States of the relevant Security Council resolutions on terrorism. The mandate derives from Security Council resolution 1373 (2001), which was renewed in its subsequent resolutions, including most recently resolution 2810 (2025), by which the Council extended the mandate until 5 January 2029. In addition, the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy and the 2022 Delhi Declaration on countering the use of new and emerging technologies for terrorist purposes set forth several tasks for the Executive Directorate with respect to facilitating the delivery of technical assistance, assessing the capacities of Member States to counter the use of new and emerging technologies for terrorist purposes, including by developing two sets of non-binding guiding principles, compiling good practices, producing a gaps analysis and promoting good counter-terrorism practices.

267.	In its resolution 2462 (2019), the Security Council requested the Executive Directorate to strengthen its assessment process relating to countering the financing of terrorism and to provide annually, on the basis of its reporting and in consultation with the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring team, to the UN Office of Counter Terrorism, through the Counterterrorism Committee, a thematic summary assessment of gaps identified and areas requiring more action to implement key counterterrorism financing provisions of relevant Council resolutions for the purpose of designing targeted technical assistance and capacity-building efforts.
Programme of work
Objective

268.	The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to enhance Member States’ counter-terrorism legislation and policies, institutions and operations by ensuring the full and effective implementation by Member States of Security Council resolution 1373 (2001) and other relevant Council resolutions, to inform the efforts of United Nations entities and other implementing agencies to provide related capacity-building and technical assistance and to analyse new and emerging terrorism threats, trends and challenges.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
269.	To contribute to the objective, the Executive Directorate will:

(a)	Assist Member States in identifying and addressing implementation and capacity gaps in accordance with the requirements of Security Council resolution 1373 (2001) and subsequent Council resolutions on terrorism, through assessments and analytical tools, including country visits, the electronic detailed implementation survey and the overview of implementation assessments, and make technical recommendations to Member States on ways to strengthen their implementation of the relevant resolutions;

(b)	Strengthen the effectiveness, timeliness and impact, as well as the transparency and inclusivity, of assessments conducted by the Executive Directorate on behalf of the Committee. This will include enhancing the assessment process relating to countering the financing of terrorism through targeted and focused follow-up visits as complements to comprehensive assessments, as well as to annual assessments of gaps and areas requiring more action to implement key provisions of Security Council resolutions relating to countering the financing of terrorism for the purpose of designing targeted technical assistance by relevant partners;

(c)	Organize follow-up meetings at the Committee level and in other bilateral and multilateral settings to highlight the priority technical assistance needs of visited Member States, and to facilitate the delivery of technical assistance;

(d)	Contribute to identifying and assessing emerging issues, trends and developments relating to relevant resolutions and in support of action 23 of the Pact for the Future, the Global Digital Compact and the Declaration on Future Generations. In this respect, it will prepare and publish analytical materials, reference tools and guidelines and promote Security Council and Committee policy papers, international standards, codes and effective practices;

(e)	Integrate and promote in the Executive Directorate’s work the non-binding guiding principles on threats posed by the use of unmanned aircraft systems for terrorist purposes, preventing, detecting and disrupting the use of new and emerging financial technologies for terrorist purposes and countering the use of ICT for terrorist purposes, which were prepared in accordance with the Delhi Declaration.
270.	The above-mentioned work is expected to result in strengthening of Member States’ capacities to:
(a)	Combat terrorism, including violent extremism conducive to terrorism and achieve the full and effective implementation of resolution 1373 (2001) and other relevant resolutions;

(b)	Take action on recommendations in Committee visit reports and other assessments and facilitate the provision of technical assistance and share effective practices with other Member States, as appropriate;

(c)	Operationalize their obligations pursuant to resolution 1373 (2001) and other relevant resolutions by facilitating awareness and understanding of the internationally recognized effective practices, techniques and tools available to combat terrorism.

271.	With respect to cooperation with other entities, the Executive Directorate cooperates with a wide range of international, regional and subregional organizations, including the Financial Action Task Force and its regional bodies, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, the Council of Europe, the European Union and the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, to raise awareness of international requirements on counter-terrorism at the national and regional levels. It leverages and further develops its Global Counter-Terrorism Research Network to convene policymakers and researchers and engages and enhances its partnerships with civil society organizations, think tanks, academic institutions and the private sector to assist the Committee in identifying national, regional and thematic challenges and developments.

272.	With respect to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Executive Directorate works closely with other United Nations entities, within the framework of the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Coordination Compact. The Executive Directorate continues to pursue efficiency gains through chairing or co-chairing Global Compact working groups and by systematically sharing the Committee’s recommendations and consented reports with the Compact, to ensure that relevant member entities participate in its assessment work and the development of prioritized recommendations as well as the design and delivery of technical assistance to build Member States’ capacity in the most pressing areas, while reducing duplication and strengthening coherence across the United Nations system and technical assistance providers. The Executive Directorate will continue to collaborate with the Office of Counter-Terrorism and UNODC on relevant issues. It works closely with other subsidiary bodies of the Security Council and their expert groups to enhance information-sharing. It maintains strong cooperation with OHCHR and the Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms while countering terrorism.
273.	With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	Consent of Member States to receive assessment visits and subsequently brief the Committee on progress made in implementing Committee recommendations;
(b)	Ability to organize and conduct visits in accordance with United Nations safety and security measures;
(c)	Ability to assess relevant thematic areas in sufficient detail, in particular to implement the mandate under operative paragraph 35 of resolution 2462 (2019);
(d) 	Participation of technical experts from international and regional organizations in country visit assessments conducted by the Executive Directorate on behalf of the Committee;
(e)	Commitment of implementing partners to deliver technical assistance pursuant to Committee findings;
(f)	Consideration by the Counter-Terrorism Committee of the non-binding guiding principles on countering the use of ICT for terrorist purposes;
(g) 	Plenary meetings of the Counter-Terrorism Committee are conducted according to schedule;
(h) 	Implementation of proposals of the Executive Directorate pursuant to paragraphs 11 and 14 of Security Council resolution 2617 (2021).

274.	The Executive Directorate integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate, and works with the Working Group on Adopting a Gender-Sensitive Approach to Preventing and Countering Terrorism.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

275.	The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects changes arising from the UN80 Initiative. In particular, the tables of deliverables reflect updated planned deliverables for 2026, in line with the approved programme budget for 2026.
Programme performance in 2025
Road maps to improve the capacity of Member States to counter terrorism and violent extremism conducive to terrorism

276.	In 2025, the Committee adopted reports on visits to ten States (Canada, Ecuador, Kazakhstan, Malta, Mauritania, Montenegro, Malawi, Tanzania, Thailand and Turkmenistan). The Executive Directorate completed five overview of implementation assessments and electronic detailed implementation surveys. It also facilitated technical assistance and developed eight road maps for select beneficiaries as part of several capacity-building programmes spearheaded by the Office of Counter-Terrorism to enhance Member States’ compliance with relevant Security Council resolutions and international standards. For instance, CTED led capacity consultations under the UN Countering Terrorist Travel Programme to help increase implementation of advance passenger information (API) and passenger name records (PNR) pursuant to Security Council resolution 2396 (2017) and ICAO standards. In 2025, CTED led seven national consultations on API/PNR, bringing the total number of Member States assessed to 49. The positive impact can be illustrated with the latest reporting of Member States using goTravel (the software provided under the Programme) who reported a significant number of hits in their passenger information units. These hits are generated through the systematic screening of API and PNR data against targeting rules as well as watchlists and law-enforcement databases. All these hits would have gone unnoticed without the capabilities that CT Travel has built in beneficiary Member States. Another Member State developed a roadmap under the Global Programme on Countering Terrorist Threats against Vulnerable Targets.

Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions
(A/80/7/Add.12)

The Advisory Committee notes the intention to reorganize the support provided to the special political missions on the basis of the workload of teams supporting sanctions panels, sanctions committees and other subsidiary organs and trusts that more information in that regard will be provided in the next report. The Committee trusts that the Secretary-General will ensure the continued implementation of mandated activities and address challenges related to the proposed level of resources. The Committee looks forward to receiving updated information on mandate implementation and comprehensive mitigation plans in the next budget submission. (para. 8)

Owing to the resource reductions under UN80 initiative, the Secretariat undertook an assessment and adjusted the workload across cluster II special political missions administered by the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, taking into account the scope and complexity of mandates, reporting requirements and the operational demands of experts and supporting staff. 
The Secretariat is continuing to assess and adjust the workload of both its programme budget and cluster II special political mission staff in light of the prevailing liquidity constraints and related hiring restrictions to ensure continued mandate implementation. 
More generally, over the past several years, the Secretariat has implemented several initiatives aimed at increasing efficiencies and mitigating against the effect of budget reductions on mandate implementation by consolidating several technical functions. Today, the Secretariat centrally manages all sanctions lists through an enhanced data model, as requested by the Security Council in paragraph 48 of resolution 2253 (2016). The Secretariat has also consolidated the administrative functions for contracting, onboarding and exit of experts and the management of its Pool of Experts, as well as functions related to the provision of training to Committee Chairs, Council members and other Member States, and will continue to seek further efficiencies wherever feasible.
For the Support to the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1540 (2004) on the non-proliferation of all weapons of mass destruction, the mission has:
Maintained full implementation of mandated activities by ensuring continuity of staffing and expert support, with five posts (1 P-5, 2 P-3, 2 GS (OL)) retained for 2027 and no changes to post levels. 
Integrated updated workload, staffing, and resource data into its 2027 budget submission, including detailed justification for operational costs, expert fees, travel, and online training requirements. 
Provided updated mitigation measures to ensure mandate delivery despite resource constraints, including prioritization of workload, enhanced planning of expert travel, and continued use of virtual engagement with Member States. 
Contributed to Cluster II–wide coordination efforts, in line with the Secretary-General’s approach to standardize and streamline support for sanctions committees and subsidiary bodies.

The Advisory Committee trusts that updated information on vacancy rates and vacant posts will be provided to the General Assembly during the consideration of its present report and in the next budget submission. (para. 11)
Information on vacancy rates is provided in Annex II to this report. Additional information on vacant posts is provided in the supplementary information submitted to the committees.

The Advisory Committee takes note of the changes in the ratio of experts to staff and trusts that the Secretariat will explore opportunities to further streamline the support resources, on the basis of a workload analysis, and that updated information thereon will be provided in future budget submissions. The Committee encourages the Secretariat to review the basing arrangement for the experts to maximize cost efficiency and mandate implementation. (para. 25)

Acting under Chapter VII, the Security Council defines the mandates of panels of experts, including the required expertise, composition and basing arrangements necessary to implement each mandate. The Secretariat’s role is to operationalize these mandates in a cost-effective manner, consistent with established budgetary and staffing policies. 
In accordance with the overall strategic vision of the Secretary-General under the UN80 initiative, the Secretariat reduced its staff and operational resource requirements under both the programme and cluster II special political mission budgets (A/800/400). In so doing, the Secretariat identified efficiencies and operational cost reductions, including, in consultations with Security Council members, a reduction in the number of experts on panels of three special political missions (Panel of Experts pursuant to resolution 2713 (2023), Panel of Experts pursuant to resolution 2745 (2024) and the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team). In addition, the basing arrangement for the Panel of Experts pursuant to resolution 2713 (2023) was changed from Nairobi to being home-based. These reductions were based on the assessment of the scope and complexity of special political mission mandates, their workload and reporting requirements (number of Chair briefings, committee meetings, informal consultations, informal-informals, number of exemptions requests, the volume of entries on the sanctions list, mandated annual review of sanctions lists, incoming and outgoing committee communications and notes, and panel missions, outreach activities, etc.), required security arrangements for experts, and the assessment of the workload of staff supporting the special political missions.
The Secretariat has reviewed the expert–staff ratio and support structure for the 1540 mandate as part of a broader Cluster II workload analysis. The existing configuration—five regular-budget posts (1 P-5, 2 P-3, 2 GS (OL)) supporting the nine experts of the Committee—was confirmed as appropriate, and no changes are proposed for 2027, while noting that the current support‑to‑expert ratio is near its functional limit and requires careful work prioritization. Updated information on this ratio and the underlying workload has been reflected in the budget submission. In addition, the mission continues to seek efficiencies through optimized travel planning, wider use of virtual engagement, and participation in Cluster II efforts to ensure cost-effective expert basing arrangements without compromising mandate implementation.
